inline.s: Samādhi is rendered in Chinese as “equal holding,” meaning that concentration and wisdom are evenly balanced. When concentration and wisdom are evenly balanced, this is called understanding. Thus understanding arises from concentration and wisdom; in other words, it is the collective name for both knowing and seeing. This agrees in meaning with the earlier phrase, “deeply understanding the meaning and purport.”

The Elder had long since attained the samādhi of non-contention, so his power of concentration was already sufficient; but his wisdom was not yet its equal. When he heard the profound prajñā, his wisdom increased and grew supreme, and so he could understand deeply. The Elder wept and wailed precisely because he was ashamed that until then he had had much concentration and little wisdom; now he was fortunate enough to hear this profound sutra and attain the even balance of concentration and wisdom. Hence his feeling was extreme, and he wept.

Since it says “understanding,” why does it also say “faith”? One should know that faith is the gate of entry to the Way and the mother of merit and virtue. Faith means accordance. Because one accords thus, one can know thus and see thus. Understanding is the collective name for knowing and seeing, and so it is called “believing and understanding thus.” Because one accords without the slightest gap with the principle that all is one suchness, and because concentration and wisdom are evenly balanced, one can avoid producing marks of dharmas. (The line “knowing thus” makes clear the power of concentration. The line “seeing thus” makes clear the power of wisdom. The line “believing and understanding thus” makes clear the power of concentration and wisdom in even balance. The word “faith” runs through all three lines. The line “not producing marks of dharmas” is the effect produced by the three lines above.)

Why is this? Because with both concentration and wisdom one accords with the one suchness. One can see that such a one is entirely free of all marks—of speech, of names, of mental conditioning. When all marks are left behind, the fundamental right wisdom is brought forth, that is, the wisdom of non-discrimination. When wisdom does not discriminate, not a single thought arises; and when not a single thought arises, this is called not producing marks of dharmas. In sum, knowing, seeing, believing, and understanding are the preparatory means to non-arising; when these means are fully cultivated one realizes the originally non-arising. All the work lies in knowing, seeing, believing, and understanding; non-arising is their effect. On the originally non-arising, no effort can be brought to bear; to fasten upon non-arising is itself arising. The next section makes this meaning clear.
(Gui) Next, non-arising is also absent.
“Subhūti, what are called marks of dharmas, the Tathāgata teaches to be no marks of dharmas; therefore they are called marks of dharmas.”

All marks of dharmas are merely provisional names; from the outset they are not. For arising is precisely non-arising. This makes clear the reason for the phrase above, “not producing marks of dharmas.” One should know that “not producing marks of dharmas” does not mean that marks of dharmas exist but are not produced, nor does it mean that in the end there are no marks of dharmas at all. It means that all marks of dharmas are from the outset conditioned productions. What is produced from conditions is empty in its very substance. As it is said, they are not absent because of any making, but because their own nature is absent. Since their own nature is absent, non-arising too is gone. Why? Because arising is precisely non-arising. This is the true meaning of non-arising. If one does not understand that their existence is precisely emptiness, and instead fixes the attention upon non-arising, then that is precisely arising: how can it be called non-arising? Therefore all who arouse the mind should, upon this one suchness, know, see, believe, and understand. This is precisely subduing; this is precisely non-abiding. If one can truly know, see, believe, and understand thus, then though marks of dharmas blaze forth in abundance, from the first they have never arisen, because their own nature is non-arising. Then without subduing one subdues; without abiding one abides; abiding yet not abiding, one enters the true nature of no-mark and no-non-mark.

Moreover, if arising is precisely non-arising, then likewise cessation is precisely non-cessation. One can see that to speak of arising and cessation, and to speak of non-arising and non-ceasing, is still to speak in terms of opposites. In truth, within unceasing arising and ceasing there is from the outset neither arising nor cessation. Not only can arising and cessation not be spoken of; even non-arising and non-ceasing cannot be spoken of. This should be contemplated with wholehearted care.

It says “the Tathāgata teaches.” The Tathāgata is the Dharma-body, and the Dharma-body is precisely true reality. Therefore the teaching is given in terms of the Tathāgata: “no marks of dharmas, therefore they are called marks of dharmas,” in order to reveal the meaning of no-mark and no-non-mark. In sum, this section makes clear that within marks of dharmas there are no marks of dharmas, and within arising there is no arising; it is not that non-arising is taken as non-arising. The meaning here is that not only is the thought of arising absent; the thought of non-arising is absent as well. This is precisely a portrait of not a single thought arising, a portrait of the originally non-arising, and a portrait of what comes below: “not grasping at marks, unmoved in suchness.” “Unmoved in suchness” is another name for arising being precisely non-arising.

Moreover, this section is also precisely the concluding revelation of the meaning stated at the opening of the sutra: “thus should one abide,” “thus should one subdue the mind.” Hence the section heading reads “concluding revelation.” It does not conclude this section alone. The entire sutra’s meaning and purport is to this point comprehensively embraced without omission, complete from head to tail.

What constitutes this concluding section? “Nowhere coming from, nowhere going to” is not producing marks of dharmas. “A unity is inexpressible” is not producing marks of dharmas. “The view of self is not, and yet is named” is not producing marks of dharmas. For it causes one, within coming and going, to be without coming and going; within unity, to be without unity; within the view of self, to be without the view of self. Why is this? Because one turns directly toward the source of mind where no thought has yet arisen, illumines it with awareness, and thereby accords with and enters the originally non-arising. As for what was said at the opening of the sutra—liberating beings yet without the mark of liberation, and so on down to “the mind like empty space”—is this not not producing marks of dharmas? And what was set forth in the introductory section, how the World-Honored One appeared in the same guise as an ordinary man and for forty-nine years did things as though he did nothing—is this not not producing marks of dharmas? All the other teachings can be threaded through with this meaning. This is what is meant by “thus should one know, thus see, thus believe and understand.” In sum, all these thousands of words and ten thousand phrases are nothing but to cause one, within all marks, to be without marks, and thereby to realize that arising is precisely non-arising. Hence it is said that the entire sutra’s meaning and purport is comprehensively embraced without omission, complete from head to tail. The orthodox part of the sutra is now concluded.

blocks.text: Chapter Thirty-Two: The Transformation Body Is Not Real

inline.s: (Yi) Three, the section on dissemination.

In marking off the section on dissemination, the ancients each had their own view. Zhiyi placed the preceding section, the concluding revelation of non-arising, into the dissemination section as well; Ouyi followed him, naming the preceding section “dissemination by entrustment” and this section “dissemination by comparison of merit.” From “how should one proclaim” onward is the method of dissemination; from “when the Buddha had spoken this sutra” onward is the manner of dissemination. Jixiang marked off only from “when the Buddha had spoken this sutra” onward as the dissemination section. Huijing, Guifeng, and Datian in the early Qing all followed him. Kuiji seems to agree, though he did not use the words “introductory, orthodox, and dissemination,” but established other names instead. Only Puwan in the early Qing thought otherwise. He wrote the Commentary on the Seal of Mind. In his commentary he tends to take many names as literal fact, because he explains in terms of the three truths. One view alone stands out beyond the rest and cannot be covered over by others: namely, that beginning from this section he marks off the dissemination section. Why call this view outstanding? The sutra says, “How should one proclaim it to others?” This line already plainly discloses the method of propagating this sutra; to mark it off as the dissemination section accords exactly with the sutra’s purport. Therefore this time we follow his division.

(Yi) This section has two parts: (Bing) first, showing and urging dissemination; next, the proper conclusion of dissemination. (Bing, first) again has two parts: (Ding) first, showing the benefit of dissemination; next, showing the method of dissemination. (Ding, first) again has two parts: (Wu) first, introducing the gift of wealth; next, explaining the gift of Dharma.
(Wu) First, introducing the gift of wealth.
“Subhūti, suppose someone were to take seven treasures filling worlds as numberless as the sands of the Ganges and use them for giving.”

Asaṃkhyeya is rendered in Chinese as “numberless.” Here it is not merely numberless; it is the numberless of the measureless. To give seven treasures filling measureless and numberless worlds—the supremacy of the merit gained can be known. The reason for introducing this gift of wealth is to show that the merit of the gift of Dharma below is still more supreme. As for the two words “take and use”: why are they not reckoned redundant in this place? Because the intent is to lead into the words below, “uphold this sutra.” The meaning is that the practice of giving may be the same while the merit differs, because what is taken up and used in the giving differs. One takes up treasures of wealth; the other takes up the treasure of Dharma. To uphold the treasures of wealth of numberless worlds does not equal upholding one scroll of the sutra, or even a four-line verse—because the gift of wealth saves only a person’s body and life, while the gift of Dharma saves a person’s wisdom-life. The gift of Dharma saves people thoroughly. Yet this is not to say that the gift of wealth may be abolished. It simply makes clear that wealth is like an illusion, like a transformation, while ordinary beings greedily cling to it, not knowing that greed and desire are endless while wealth is exhaustible. If one understands the Buddhadharma, one knows that all worldly affairs are nothing but a dream, an illusion. Those who receive the gift of wealth may thereby escape suffering, and those who practice the gift of wealth have their merit increased as well. Moreover, among all conditioned dharmas, wealth is the hardest to see through, and so it is introduced here as the topic. Wherever wealth-giving is brought forward for comparison as the lesser, the intent is the same. This should be understood accordingly.
(Wu) Next, explaining the gift of Dharma.

“If a good man or good woman who has aroused the bodhisattva mind upholds this sutra, even so much as a four-line verse, receives and upholds it, reads and recites it, and proclaims it to others, that merit surpasses the former.”

The ancient editions and the Song canon all read “who has aroused the bodhisattva mind.” In the current circulating edition, “bodhisattva” has become “bodhi.” One should follow the ancient text. Why? The sutra says: one who, not yet having saved himself, first wishes to save others, has aroused the bodhisattva mind. What is called dissemination lays its weight on the gift of Dharma benefiting the many. Hence it says “arousing the bodhisattva mind,” to reveal the meaning of dissemination. One should know that the bodhi mind has a very broad meaning and is not limited to the one matter of the gift of Dharma. Here, because the method of dissemination is about to be pointed out, the arousing of the bodhisattva mind is singled out for mention. It precisely echoes the line below, “how should one proclaim it to others.”

As for “a four-line verse and so on,” the “and so on” extends to half a verse, or a single line. Four lines make one verse; two lines make half a verse. The sutras often say that half a verse suffices to realize the Way. If one can believe, accept, and practice the half verse spoken below—“not grasping at marks, unmoved in suchness”—one goes straight to the jeweled city. How much more so a whole verse, and how much more so the whole sutra.

The “uphold” in “upholds this sutra” means to take up and hold. It differs in meaning from “receive and uphold” below. The phrase “receives and upholds” is self-benefit; the phrase “proclaims” is benefit for others. If one receives and upholds it in accordance with the Dharma, one can awaken to and enter non-arising, give without abiding in marks, and that merit alone already surpasses the former. How much more when one further proclaims this sutra to others, practicing the gift of Dharma that does not abide in marks. For this sutra says in its opening chapter that one should liberate boundless beings into remainderless nirvana; to proclaim this sutra to others now is precisely to give the Dharma of remainderless nirvana as a gift. How could the gift of seven treasures compare? The opening chapter also says that giving does not abide in marks. Then those who hear this teaching of non-abiding will surely not limit their giving to seven treasures filling numberless worlds. In sum, to propagate this sutra is to perpetuate and exalt the Buddha-seed. The benefit to beings is inconceivable. That its merit surpasses the gift of wealth needs no saying. The sutra’s purport lays its weight on disseminating the supreme treasure of Dharma, and so below it speaks exclusively in terms of proclaiming. Moreover, once one understands how to proclaim, one understands of itself how to receive and uphold. Speak of the one side, and both sides are encompassed.
(Ding) Next, showing the method of dissemination. This has two parts: (Wu) first, pointing directly to the original nature; next, contemplating the conditioning of dharmas.
(Wu) First, pointing directly to the original nature.
“How should one proclaim it to others? Not grasping at marks, unmoved in suchness.”

“How should one proclaim it to others?” is a question. It contains two meanings. First, it asks how the one who proclaims should be. Second, it asks how the meaning of the sutra should be proclaimed. The two lines “not grasping at marks, unmoved in suchness” precisely set forth the rule that both should observe. As for the speaker: he should grasp at none of the marks of the one who speaks, the words spoken, or those who hear. This is what is meant by “with a mind neither arising nor ceasing, proclaim the Dharma of true reality.” This sutra is precisely the Dharma of true reality, and so the speaker should speak it with a mind neither arising nor ceasing. The mind neither arising nor ceasing is the original nature; this is what is meant by “unmoved in suchness.” The sense is that one who proclaims the profound prajñā should be empty of the three wheels, and should speak in accordance with the nature, pointing directly to the source of mind. Only thus can he cause hearers, by means of the prajñā of words, to bring forth the prajñā of contemplation and awaken to the prajñā of true reality. The words imply that one must neither speak wildly nor speak shallowly.

Spoken with reference to proclaiming this sutra: the meaning and purport of this sutra is most profound and most vast. Earlier it was said that all Buddhas come forth from this sutra. Then all that is spoken in the sutra is the Dharma of becoming a Buddha. Its profundity can be known. It also says that the Dharma of the Buddhas’ anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi all comes forth from this sutra. Then all Buddhadharma spoken in the sutra lies within it. Its vastness can be known. So if one wishes to proclaim it to others, unless one gains the essential method, one will either be grand but ineffectual or scattered without return, and hearers will find it hard to gain the benefit of Dharma. Therefore the essential point of the sutra’s meaning is shown: namely, the two lines and one verse that follow. One can see that these two lines and one verse are the essential purport of this sutra, and also the essential purport of all Buddhadharma. The nature, cultivation, principle, and phenomena spoken of in a thousand sutras and ten thousand treatises are all embraced and exhausted by these two lines and one verse.

There is something further. On the surface this instructs on how to proclaim; beneath the surface it instructs on how to receive and uphold. How is this said? For to proclaim thus, one must first be able to receive and uphold thus; otherwise, how could one proclaim it? And to proclaim it to others is precisely to wish others to receive and uphold it thus. This should be understood accordingly. From this we see clearly that the meaning of the two lines, “not grasping at marks, unmoved in suchness,” is deep and vast. Now they should be opened out layer by layer.

First, one should know that these two lines are the concluding words of the whole sutra and also its revealing words. What is meant by concluding? In this entire sutra, from first to last, all that is spoken is nothing but the meaning of not grasping. This is clear at a glance; it needs no citation, and citations would be inexhaustible. When it says “all dharmas are thus,” “neither real nor unreal,” “all dharmas are Buddhadharma,” “all dharmas are equal,” and so on—all these are the meaning of suchness. “Nowhere coming from, nowhere going to” is the meaning of unmoved. Here these two lines simply bring the meaning of the whole sutra to a close. This is what is meant by concluding words.

Then why are they also called revealing words? What the whole sutra says, though it is all this one meaning, appears scattered here and there. If a student cannot weave it together, he will gaze at the ocean and sigh, not knowing where to enter. Therefore it is revealed and declared: the essential point of the whole sutra is nothing other than the eight words “not grasping at marks, unmoved in suchness.” Students should enter from here. Only then can hearers grasp the essential and set to work, no longer looking before and behind or drifting without return. This is what is meant by revealing words.

Second, one should know that these two lines speak both of the work of cultivation and of its effect. For one must be able not to grasp before one can be unmoved; yet one must also be able to contemplate unmovedness before one can not grasp. They are, as it is said, mutually cause and effect. If one takes only non-grasping as the work of cultivation, the sutra’s meaning becomes one-sided and incomplete. Now they will be explained in the order of the text.

As for “marks”: marks of adornment, marks of merit, marks of beings, marks of liberating beings, marks of bodhi, marks of arousing the mind, marks of seeking marks, marks of transforming those below, marks of cause, marks of effect, and so on—the count would never end. In sum, wherever a dharma is spoken of, it has its mark. Here they are summed up in one phrase: whatever marks there are, none are grasped. One should know that in speaking of the one word “marks,” both dharmas and non-dharmas are included. Therefore the words “not grasping at marks” also run through to not annihilating marks. Why? Annihilation is the mark of emptiness, and it too is not to be grasped. This should be understood accordingly. This is what is meant by seeing the other side from this side. In reading Buddhist sutras, this principle is the first thing to know. If “not grasping at marks” is not understood in this way, it will not accord with the line below, “unmoved in suchness.”

Why? Because if one leans even slightly toward either emptiness or existence, it is not suchness. And why is that? Because leaning means grasping, and grasping means one is already moved. In sum, whatever the grasping, grasping moves the mind; grasping clings to marks and is no longer the nature of suchness. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says, “All grasping and rejecting is saṃsāra.” Saṃsāra means the mind of arising and ceasing. If there is grasping, there must be rejecting. Grasping and rejecting come from discrimination and attachment—what is called the mind of arising and ceasing. Therefore it says, “All grasping and rejecting is saṃsāra,” which is to say that all grasping and rejecting comes from the mind of discrimination and attachment that arises and ceases. If one can then avoid grasping, one is at once free of the mind of arising and ceasing, and at once sees the nature that neither arises nor ceases. Hence it says: not grasping at marks, unmoved in suchness.

“Unmoved in suchness” is the nature that neither arises nor ceases. “Not grasping” is the true explanation of non-abiding. Non-abiding is the true explanation of unmovedness. Why? If the mind abides, then it does not abide. The words “does not abide” precisely show that it moves. “If the mind abides, then it does not abide” is to say that to grasp is for the mind to move. Therefore one must grasp nothing at all, and only then be moved by nothing at all. “Suchness” is another name for true suchness; both mean the original nature. The reason two names are set up is that true suchness speaks of what is originally possessed, while suchness speaks of what is realized. For when one realizes the nature, outside wisdom there is no principle and outside principle no wisdom. Wisdom and principle merge in the dark, and this is called wisdom being thus and principle being thus—hence “suchness.” The meaning of suchness makes clear that both subject and object are gone. Because there is no realizing and nothing realized, one is utterly freed from the faculties and their objects, and the spiritual light shines alone. Therefore stillness and illumination are simultaneous. Because it is still while illuminating and illuminating while still, there are no marks and no non-marks. Because both marks and non-marks are absent, there is neither arising nor ceasing. Because there is neither arising nor ceasing, it is unmoved in suchness. Now, since one does not grasp the marks of arising and ceasing, the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, of unmoved suchness, appears before one. Hence it says: not grasping at marks, unmoved in suchness.

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All sentient beings’ beginningless illusory ignorance is established from the perfect-enlightenment mind of the Tathāgatas. It is like flowers in empty space, which depend on space and have their marks; when the flowers in space vanish, space itself is unmoved.” The perfect-enlightenment mind of the Tathāgatas is the original nature shared alike by Buddhas and beings. In the portion of sentient beings it is called the Tathāgata-garbha. This line speaks in terms of sages and ordinary beings together, not of the Buddha alone. (If it spoke of the Buddha alone, the preceding line could not hold.) “Like flowers in empty space, which depend on space and have their marks” illustrates how beings, from beginningless time, because of non-awakening, depend on the originally empty and still nature and illusorily form the marks of ignorance. From this one may know that ignorance is merely an illusory mark arisen from conditions within the original nature, like a flower in space. Space originally has no flower; therefore the nature originally has no ignorance—this is clear. “When the flowers in space vanish, space itself is unmoved” illustrates how, when ignorance ceases, the nature is originally unmoved. “Originally unmoved” means that even when ignorance is presently present, this nature has never once moved. One should know that what is ordinarily called the movement of the mind is only the movement of ignorance. From this one may understand all the more clearly the principle that if one can simply not grasp at marks, the originally unmoved nature of suchness appears at once. One may also know that grasping and rejecting come precisely from ignorance, and that ignorance is itself an illusory mark. Therefore one who does not grasp at marks is at once unmoved in suchness, because there is no grasping or rejecting and ignorance has already been dispelled. For this reason students should apply themselves bitterly to non-grasping, which is non-abiding. Otherwise, though they wish not to grasp, it cannot be attained.

As for the two words “suchness,” some explain the first “thus” as “similar” and “corresponding,” and the second “thus” as “true suchness”: that only when one does not grasp at marks is one similar and corresponding to the true-suchness original nature, and the mind unmoved. This explanation is not sound. The Compendium of the Meaning of the Great Vehicle plainly says that suchness is also true suchness. Moreover, the name “suchness” is constantly met with in the Mahāyāna sutras, and mostly refers to the Buddha’s realm. How could it mean “similar and corresponding”? Even if one wished to divide it and explain the two separately, the first “thus” could be explained as “accordance”—according with true suchness, what is called the dark merging of wisdom and principle. But if one says “similar” or “corresponding,” then the essence remains the essence and the wisdom remains the wisdom, and the marks of subject and object stand plainly before one. How could that be “not grasping at marks”? Therefore this explanation, at first glance, merely seems shallow; examined closely, it is grossly inconsistent. Hence it is called unsound.

The Buddha said, “Free from illusion, that is enlightenment.” The word “enlightenment” precisely means the nature of unmoved suchness. The word “that is” precisely means that it is so right now. One can see that the only fear is being unable not to grasp. If one can truly not grasp, it is already accomplished right now. To explain it instead as “not grasping at marks, yet similar to the nature” plainly contradicts the Buddha’s words and must never be followed.

A moment ago it was said that students should apply themselves bitterly to the two words “not grasping.” Then how can one not grasp? This layer must not be passed over in neglect; it must be examined carefully. One should know that not grasping at marks is being free of marks. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All bodhisattvas and beings of the final age should keep far from all illusory and false realms. Because of firmly holding the mind of keeping far away, the mind that is like an illusion is also kept far away. Keeping far away is itself illusion, so that too is kept far away. The illusion of keeping far away is also kept far away. When one reaches having nothing to keep far from, all illusions are removed.” Examining the meaning of this passage carefully, one can see that the work of freedom from marks lies wholly in firm holding. Firm holding means forcible restraint. This layer of work is truly indispensable; otherwise, how could the habit of grasping at marks from beginningless time be removed?

Yet one should examine still more carefully: how can one firmly hold to non-grasping? If one wishes to know how firm holding in non-grasping is possible, one must first know why sentient beings grasp. There is no other reason: it is because they have a discriminating mind that attaches to the four marks of self, person, being, and life. And one should further know that the marks of these four are in fact nothing but the one mark of self, and that the root of the mark of self in fact arises from the view of self.

One should examine with particular care: firmly holding to non-grasping is indeed sufficient to dispel the view of self, but it can only suppress it, not cut it off. Why? Because ignorance has not yet been broken. Moreover, because the ignorance and the view of self are not cut off, they are precisely what most easily destroys that firm holding. Then one cannot but work further at being free of ignorance and the view of self. How can one be free of them? The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, quoted earlier, says: “Knowing illusion, one is at once free of it; no preparatory means are used.” The two words “knowing illusion” are the most wonderful preparatory means for being free of ignorance; there is no need to seek any other means.

Then how can one know that it is illusion? The Śūraṅgama Sutra is clearest on this. It says: “When the Tathāgata first aroused the mind on the causal ground, he first used the direct mind to be mindful of true suchness, and only then could he keep far from all illusions.” Right mindfulness is illuminating awareness. It means one must directly illuminate with awareness the true-suchness original nature, and only then can one know that it is illusion. From this one can see that one must first awaken to the originally unmoved nature of suchness before one can avoid grasping at marks. This is why it was said above that the two lines “not grasping at marks, unmoved in suchness” are mutually cause and effect, and should be practiced in alternation. One must not take the line on non-grasping as the work of cultivation and the line on suchness as the effect alone.

In other words, one must not only hold firm in non-grasping; one must also illuminate with awareness in suchness. Moreover, illuminating awareness is the preparatory means to firm holding: to hold firm in non-grasping, one must first cultivate illuminating awareness. Otherwise, with ignorance uncut, how could one hold firm? Therefore the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All bodhisattvas and beings of the final age should first cut off the beginningless root of saṃsāra.” The root of saṃsāra means ignorance and the view of self. Then how is it cut off? Does not the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, quoted earlier, say: “All Tathāgatas, when they first aroused the mind on the causal ground, relied on perfect illumination of the pure mark of enlightenment, forever cut off ignorance, and only then accomplished the Buddha Way.” This agrees in meaning with the passage quoted from the Śūraṅgama Sutra about first using the direct mind to be mindful of true suchness.

Take the example of a wicked friend. At first, through ignorance, one mistook him for a bosom companion. Now that one knows his wickedness, one wishes to break with him; but because the bond is long-standing, one cannot cut it off all at once. One must first draw away from him, and only then can one break with him. It is the same here. From beginningless time one has mistaken the ignorance of the illusory consciousness for one’s true mind, and the bond has been close and long. Now that one has suddenly awakened and knows it to be wrong, if one does not at once turn one’s head around, recognize the pure self-nature, and go straight to draw near it, one will still be mixed in with ignorance. Therefore perfect illumination of the mark of enlightenment is precisely the direct mind mindful of true suchness; it is drawing near the true mind. And drawing near the true mind is drawing away from ignorance. Only thus can one hope to cut it off forever.

Therefore the crucial work lies wholly in the two words “perfect illumination.” What is perfect illumination? The preceding thought has ceased and the following thought has not yet arisen. Just at such a moment, the single mind is deeply still, perfectly clear and bright—this is what is meant by illumination. “Perfect” means neither exerting effort nor not exerting effort, neither sinking nor floating, like a solitary bright moon perfectly round. At this point not a single thought has arisen; it is incomparably pure, and the whole body is cool—this is the original face. Beginners have no power of concentration. In a single instant the following thought arises again; then one again illumines with awareness in this way. As long as illuminating awareness can be taken up, it is like a balance: when this side rises, the other of itself falls, and one is pure again. One must make it dense and unbroken, so that it continues without interval. After a long time one can enter concentration. As for the whole body of unmoved suchness, how could it be easily and suddenly made to appear in full? Yet practicing in this way is to accord with it and move toward it. These two lines of the sutra are precisely this meaning. One must not only hold firm in non-grasping; one should also illuminate with awareness in suchness. This is crucial, crucial.

Now the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment is quoted again to prove the meaning that illuminating awareness of the original nature can remove ignorance. The sutra says: “Within non-arising, one falsely sees arising and ceasing.” This says that the self-nature is originally non-arising; being originally non-arising is being originally unmoved. Arising and ceasing here refers to ignorance. The sense is that within the self-nature there is originally no ignorance; the speaking of ignorance is due to false seeing. If this is so, then the present awareness that illuminates the pure nature is right view. Wrong and right do not stand together. When right view flourishes, false seeing is removed. Hence that sutra also says: “When the Tathāgata on the causal ground cultivates perfect enlightenment, knowing these to be empty flowers, there is no turning about. Nor are there body and mind undergoing that birth-and-death. It is not that they are absent because of making; it is that their own nature is absent.” Birth-and-death here means arising and ceasing. This says that since the self-nature is originally non-arising, it is also non-ceasing; hence “their own nature is absent.” As for there being no body and mind undergoing that birth-and-death, this is because the original nature is without arising and ceasing; it is not that making causes them to be absent. Therefore, upon arousing the mind one should illuminate with awareness the nature that is originally non-arising.

Hence it says, “on the causal ground cultivate perfect enlightenment.” The causal ground refers to the time of arousing the mind and cultivating practice. The word “cultivate” refers to illuminating awareness. “Perfect enlightenment” refers to the nature that is originally non-arising. One who cultivates thus knows that all the illusory marks of arising and ceasing are entirely empty flowers, because their existence is no existence. Knowing this, one is not turned about by them. Not being turned about makes clear that one is unmoved. Hence it says, “knowing these to be empty flowers, there is no turning about.” These two lines have the same meaning as “knowing illusion, one is at once free of it.” Since one is at once free of illusion, neither body nor mind undergoes that birth-and-death, and the Dharma-nature is suchness. Looking over the sutra passages quoted above as a whole, it should be clear that illuminating awareness directly at the place of original non-arising is the wonderful method for removing ignorance.

What is the place of original non-arising? It is illuminating with awareness at the moment before a thought has arisen. If a thought has not even arisen, what mark can there be? How much less any grasping? If one can be thus dense and unbroken, one will of itself have a sure grasp of non-grasping. In sum, on the one hand one gathers the mind and illuminates with awareness at the place of unmovedness, thereby accomplishing non-grasping; on the other hand, when meeting conditions, one holds firm in non-grasping, thereby perfecting unmovedness. Only thus can one find a place of entry into the substance of the suchness nature. The Śūraṅgama Sutra says the same. It says: “All cultivators who fail to accomplish the supreme bodhi, and even become śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or members of Māra’s retinue, do so because they do not know the two kinds of root and practice in confusion. What are the two? The first is the beginningless root of birth-and-death: namely, that you and all beings now take the mind that climbs upon conditions as your own nature. The second is the beginningless bodhi and nirvana, the originally pure substance: namely, that your own essential brightness, capable of producing all conditions, is what you have overlooked. Because beings overlook this original brightness, though they act all day they are unaware, and vainly fall into the destinies.”

The “mind that climbs upon conditions” spoken of here is the mind of non-awakening and false movement. “The originally pure substance,” down to “what you have overlooked,” is the originally unmoved nature of suchness. That sutra also says: “How is it that you now take movement as your body and movement as your surroundings, so that from beginning to end, thought after thought arises and ceases, you lose your true nature, and act in inverted ways? The nature and the mind lose the true, and you take things as yourself; you turn about within it and of yourself seize upon the wheel of birth-and-death.” This passage speaks even more plainly. That is, from the first arousing of the mind one should distinguish the true from the false and look directly toward illuminating with awareness at the place of original unmovedness. Only thus will one not overlook this original brightness, vainly fall into the destinies, and of oneself seize upon the wheel of birth-and-death.

One should know that such illuminating awareness also requires gathering the mind. Gathering the mind is not having no thoughts, nor is it in the end without marks and without grasping. Yet for ordinary beings there is no other place of entry; this is what is called the method of using illusion to remove illusion. For though this method is itself illusion, it accords with true suchness. Because the mind differs from that of those who move thoughts and grasp marks, the fruit gained differs greatly. Moreover, this method is only a preparatory means of entry. Though it is a method according with true suchness, the illuminating and the illuminated should also be progressively purified away. As it is said, having illumination and having observation are both called hindrances. Therefore one must be free of it and free again, until one reaches having nothing to be free of; then all illusions are removed. This should be understood accordingly.

In sum: “unmoved in suchness” is the meaning of non-arising; “not grasping at marks” is the meaning of non-abiding. One must first illuminate with awareness the originally non-arising, and only then can one be non-abiding. And when one abides nowhere at all, one realizes non-arising. Practicing the two in alternation is the essential gate. Moreover, practicing thus is carried through to the very end. From the first step of entry, on through the stages of abiding, practice, dedication, the grounds, equal enlightenment, and wonderful enlightenment, none is outside this. Hence it says: “Free of all marks, one is called a Buddha,” and “all Buddhas come forth from this sutra.” And the fact that the Śūraṅgama and the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment were especially quoted above to prove this meaning is enough to show that the Dharma of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi all comes forth from this sutra.

There is something further. This sutra takes breaking the self by non-abiding as its one and only purport. One can see that the entire sutra expounds the meaning that, in order to break ignorance, one should not grasp at marks. The latter half speaks of the one suchness of all dharmas and of all being equal, and so on; this expounds the meaning of unmoved suchness. Then it causes one to penetrate the selfless Dharma, and this penetration first causes one to open the Buddha’s knowing and seeing. Afterward it fully unfolds the meaning that what is conditioned is empty by nature. Since this section uses the two lines on non-grasping to instruct students to illuminate with awareness the originally unmoved nature of suchness, the next section again instructs them to contemplate the conditioning of dharmas. This exactly agrees with the purport of the latter half of the orthodox part, which first reveals suchness and then speaks of conditioning. This precisely indicates that the essential purport of the whole sutra lies in the latter half.

If one who proclaims it does not understand the meaning of the latter half, the former half will not be grasped in its essentials; and if one who receives and upholds it does not know how to enter contemplation from what the latter half teaches, he too will not grasp the essentials. This is the World-Honored One’s profound intent, and it should be deeply appreciated. As for the fact that this section causes one to illuminate with awareness the original nature while the next causes one to contemplate the conditioning of dharmas, this is all the more skillful, all the more essential. This is precisely the Buddha’s knowing and the Buddha’s seeing, and students should urgently penetrate it thus.

For ordinary beings are wholly ignorance. Though one speaks of illuminating with awareness the original nature, the face of that nature has long been hidden, and there is nothing but pitch-black ignorance. What then is to be done? Now it is instructed: one should first contemplate the conditioning of dharmas as a preparatory means. Hence the concluding words of the next section, “one should contemplate thus,” mean that one must contemplate in this way. Why? To contemplate the conditioning of dharmas is to contemplate the empty mark of all dharmas. When marks are empty, how could there be grasping? Then one is unmoved in suchness. Can this not be called skillful? Can this not be called essential? This meaning will be discussed in fuller detail in the next section.

The word “proclaim” carries a deep meaning. “Proclaim” means to unfold and develop. It means that the sutra’s meaning is dark and deep, and that one who speaks the sutra should open out its subtle points, bring forth what is hidden, and broadly cite and widely draw upon to make it known. One must make its meaning flow freely in every direction, and only then will the speaking not have been in vain. In speaking any sutra, one should follow this rule.
(Wu) Next, contemplating the conditioning of dharmas.
“Why? All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning; thus should one contemplate them.”
“Why” asks the reason for not grasping at marks. The reason has two meanings:
(1) For what reason does one not grasp? The first three lines of the verse suffice to answer this.
(2) How is one able not to grasp? This requires the whole verse to answer, with the weight on the fourth line. Now a question and answer are set up to make this clear.

Question: For what reason does one not grasp? Answer: Because all conditioned things and marks arise when conditions gather and cease when conditions scatter. Their changes are without constancy and cannot be seized or held. Like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew, or lightning, they seem to exist but are without substance.

Question: Then how can one not grasp? Answer: One should contemplate all conditioned dharmas as like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew, or lightning, knowing that in their very substance they are empty, and so not give rise to greed or attachment; only thus can one not grasp.
From what has been said above, the main purport of this section is clear. Now it will be explained in detail.

One should know that unmoved suchness is true reality; that is, the unconditioned dharma that neither arises nor ceases. It was said earlier: all sages and worthies differ by virtue of the unconditioned dharma. Now, instead of causing one to contemplate the true nature of unmoved suchness, the unconditioned dharma, it causes one to contemplate the illusory marks of conditioned dharmas, which are conditioned and without substance. Why is this? Because our World-Honored One well knew the disease of ordinary beings and specially opened a skillful means. There are two essential meanings here:

(1) The reason ordinary beings are ordinary beings is nothing else: they turn their backs on enlightenment, join with dust, and seek outside themselves. Why do they seek outside? Nothing else: they discriminate among illusory marks and greedily cling to them. Why do they discriminate and cling? Nothing else: they mistake all conditioned dharmas for real. For this reason they grow more deluded the deeper they go, refuse to turn back, and are forever caught in the turning about. Therefore, at the first step of entry, one must first cause them to contemplate deeply all conditioned dharmas—like a dream, like an illusion, like a bubble, like a shadow, like dew, like lightning—none of them true, all of them empty, so that in the end not one thing is obtained. What is obtained is only a taste of bitterness. And that bitterness is endless and beyond words. This is what is meant by “ten thousand things you cannot take with you; only karma follows the body.” If one can constantly contemplate thus and clearly understand the principle that all is empty, one may perhaps no longer be deceived, and may be able to turn the light around with all one’s heart. This is why, wishing to contemplate the true nature of the unconditioned, one should first contemplate the illusory marks of the conditioned. This first essential meaning must be understood.

(2) The light of the nature of all ordinary beings has long been covered over by ignorance. It is like a single bright sun wholly veiled by dark clouds, its light utterly dimmed, so that the sun cannot be seen. It is the same here. False thoughts stir in confusion without a moment’s pause. If one now wishes to contemplate, the contemplating and the contemplated are both ignorance and false consciousness. How could one see the original nature? This is the same principle as when the whole sky is black with clouds and the sunlight cannot be seen: look as one may, there is nothing but a dizzy, turbid appearance. Hence the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “With a mind of saṃsāra, producing a view of saṃsāra, one enters the Tathāgata’s great sea of quiescent extinction—and in the end one cannot arrive.”

“Saṃsāra” means arising and ceasing. “Quiescent” means soundless: it says that true suchness cannot be explained in words. “Extinct” means formless: it says that true suchness cannot be revealed by marks. Vertically exhausting the three periods and horizontally pervading the ten directions is called “great.” The essence complete in ten thousand virtues and the function embracing the ten thousand existents is called “sea.” The Tathāgata’s great sea of quiescent extinction means the originally unmoved nature of suchness. Pitiable are ordinary beings, who are wholly the mind of arising and ceasing. Even when they arouse the mind to contemplate, it is the view of arising and ceasing. Now, to use this mind and view of arising and ceasing to contemplate the perfect-enlightenment sea of nature that neither arises nor ceases is entirely to turn the back on it. Hence it says one cannot arrive. “Cannot arrive” means one is driving south while the cart heads north.

Then does one who cultivates perfect enlightenment, wishing to illuminate with awareness the unmoved nature of suchness, truly have no place to begin? Our World-Honored One in his great compassion now tells us: do not worry, there is a wonderful method. What is that method? One should contemplate the conditioning of all dharmas, and of itself there will be a place of entry. The sense of this is no different from saying: at first one need not forcibly still false thoughts—though one wished to still them, it could not be done.

One need only turn toward all conditioned dharmas, which involve making and duality, and observe their ceaseless change, like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew, or lightning. This causes the mind to understand clearly that all dharmas are nothing but, when conditions meet, the presently existing illusory mark of arising; in truth, arising is precisely non-arising. From this one may know that though on the surface the myriad appearances stand in dense array, at bottom they are wholly nonexistent. Contemplating and illuminating with awareness thus at every time and in every place brings inconceivable merit and virtue.

What is meant by inconceivable merit and virtue? One should know that in contemplating the principle of the conditioning of all dharmas, if one comprehends that all dharmas are empty in their very substance, one can accord with and enter the empty mark of all dharmas. When marks are empty, the nature of itself appears. Why? With marks, all dharmas are vastly different; with marks empty, all dharmas are one suchness. All dharmas being one suchness is the light of the nature appearing. The light of the nature appearing is ignorance already illuminated. Though ignorance may not yet be suddenly cut off, and may not yet suddenly merge with unmoved suchness, yet the dark merging of wisdom and principle is truly founded on this. Why? Because false thoughts from this point daily grow thinner, and when facing objects and meeting conditions one is not easily turned by them. From this we may say: to contemplate the conditioning of all dharmas is no different from contemplating the empty mark of all dharmas; to contemplate the empty mark of all dharmas is no different from contemplating unmoved suchness. In other words, to contemplate the conditioned dharmas of arising and ceasing as like a dream, like an illusion, is imperceptibly to be led into the unconditioned dharma that neither arises nor ceases. How could such merit and virtue be conceived? This second essential meaning is what we should understand even more.

Taking these two essential meanings together, one can see that to contemplate thus is like using a crane: four ounces can lift a thousand catties, without the least effort. Lightly and deftly, one parts the clouds and mist and sees the blue sky. Truly a skillful means.

Since this unworthy one began to study the Buddha’s teaching, in the first twenty years, though I practiced various methods and did various contemplations, I made no progress at all. One day, on these four lines of verse, I seemed suddenly to awaken. I practiced contemplation accordingly. At first it was half near and half far, half clear and half dim, not forming any continuous stretch, and without much effect. Then I understood that one should apply the mind with utmost effort to observe in every circumstance and condition. Even in the smallest matter, whether at a time of great contentment or great discontent, one should seal it with the principle that all is like a dream, an illusion. Even in practicing the Buddhadharma, one should seal it with the same principle. Walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, one does not depart from this. After a long time, though my work at not grasping at marks and being unmoved in suchness is still shallow, from the time I began this contemplation my mind has gradually felt empty and hollow: toward all circumstances and marks I am gradually able to remain unmoved within. In reading sutras my eyes feel a little brighter; in reciting the Buddha’s name I also feel a little more solid. Now I ask you all to try it; you will surely find it useful. One should know that for an ordinary being of this dusty world, wishing to turn the light around, there is no place to begin apart from this. Treasure it, treasure it.
Now the meaning of the preceding section and of this section will be set forth together.

The unmoved suchness spoken above is the perfect manifestation of the substance of the nature. To speak of its ultimate extent, one must reach the Buddha-stage before it can be perfect. From the first abiding stage upward it is only partially manifested; hence it is called the enlightenment of partial realization. As for those in the stage of faith, they only obtain its semblance—what is called the enlightenment of resemblance. Hence some earlier teachers explained the first “thus” above as “similar.” Yet the meaning of the line “unmoved in suchness” runs from the first arousing of the mind through to the very end without break. Therefore it should not be rigidly explained as “similar.” It should be explained as true suchness, and only then can it perfectly embrace all. Whether appearing as resemblance, as partial realization, or even as perfect manifestation, all comes from not grasping at marks. Therefore the words “marks” and “not grasping” likewise contain a deep and vast meaning and run through to the very end.

As for “marks,” whether emptiness, existence, both, or neither, all are included. The general mark of them is the two attachments, to self and to dharmas. Toward all these marks, not attaching at all is what is meant by not grasping. And even non-grasping is itself not grasped. Then one is free of it and free again; reaching having nothing to be free of, all illusions are removed. Thereupon the substance of the unmoved nature of suchness is fully revealed.

Yet the method of beginning must be to illuminate with awareness at the place where no thought has yet moved—that is, to contemplate the originally unmoved nature of suchness. This is the meaning of the Śūraṅgama Sutra’s taking the neither-arising-nor-ceasing as the cause of cultivation, and also the meaning of cultivating cessation based on the originally still nature, and thereby attaining concentration, and cultivating observation based on the originally illuminating nature, and thereby attaining wisdom. If one does not know to begin from here, one is practicing in confusion, cultivating blindly and refining in the dark—like boiling sand to make rice, which can never succeed.

Though the beginner is wholly ignorance and cannot see it by contemplating, he must deeply understand this principle and diligently practice perfect illumination. As said before: when the preceding thought has ceased and the following thought has not yet arisen, just at such a moment the single mind is deeply still, perfectly clear and bright—this is what is meant by illumination. “Perfect” means neither exerting effort nor not exerting effort, neither sinking nor floating. This is the single thread of wisdom-light, the first preparatory means for knowing illusion and being at once free of it. On the other hand, one follows this verse and contemplates all dharmas as like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew, or lightning—conditioned and therefore empty. This method is an even more preparatory means within preparatory means; it is what is called knowing illusion. The two are best cultivated together.

These two methods mutually complete each other. For illuminating with awareness the original nature is working at the root, while contemplating all dharmas is working at circumstances and conditions. Moreover, the former contemplation is mostly intended as cultivating concentration; the latter is mostly intended as cultivating wisdom. Concentration can indeed produce wisdom, yet unless wisdom is first opened, that concentration cannot be accomplished either. Therefore, in their mutual assistance, the contemplation of conditioning is especially important, since by contemplating conditioning one can be led into unmoved suchness. This meaning has already been set forth in detail above.

Consider the line “thus should one contemplate them”: it carries a strong sense that nothing else will do. How earnest it is! The word “contemplate” is crucial; it means one should apply the mind with the fullest intent to observe.

The Buddha spoke this sutra originally for ordinary beings who have aroused the great mind. These two lines and one verse precisely point out where ordinary beings of the great mind should begin their work. Therefore the two contemplations, before and after, must be practiced dense and unbroken, alternating with each other. Practiced long, one will surely find a place of attainment.

The two words “thus” certainly refer to what was said above—like a dream, like an illusion. One should know that “like a dream, like an illusion” precisely means that the marks of all dharmas are originally empty; it also precisely means that the nature of all dharmas is one suchness. One can see that the words “thus” truly contain the flavor of “one suchness in all.” Therefore, to contemplate the conditioning of all dharmas is to be able to accord with and enter unmoved suchness. One who practices this contemplation can go to the bottom with a single pole and see the original nature through. Hence it says, “thus should one contemplate them,” which is to say: to contemplate all dharmas as like a dream, like an illusion, is to contemplate the one suchness in all; therefore one should practice it. The instruction is earnest and repeated—how could one pass over it in neglect?

Conditioned dharmas are not only worldly dharmas; Buddhadharma too is included. Hence it says “all.” The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream of yesterday. No arising, no ceasing; no coming, no going. What is realized has no gain, no loss, no grasping, no rejecting. What realizes has no making, no stopping, no bearing, no extinction. Within this realization there is neither subject nor object. Ultimately there is no realization, and no one who realizes. The nature of all dharmas is equal and indestructible.” In this passage all is viewed as a dream and thereby dissolved. This is precisely what is meant by the empty mark of all dharmas, that is, the meaning of not grasping at marks. It also instructs one to contemplate all things as dream-like and so empty them, thereby according with and entering unmoved suchness. Hence it concludes: “The nature of all dharmas is equal and indestructible.” Equality is suchness; indestructibility is unmovedness. Therefore this passage of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment may fittingly be cited as a footnote to the two lines and one verse of this sutra.

In sum, whether defiled dharmas or pure dharmas: once there is such a dharma, there is duality. Once duality is established, it is conditioned and has arising and ceasing. Therefore all are like a dream, like an illusion. Yet if one wishes to realize the unconditioned dharma beyond duality, one cannot but begin cultivation from the conditioned dharma of duality, because apart from this there is no place of entry.

Not only is contemplating conditioning a conditioned dharma; even illuminating with awareness of the original nature is a conditioned dharma. Why? Because illuminating awareness is contemplation, and once there is a contemplating subject and a contemplated object, duality is established. With duality there are marks, and one falls into the conditioned.

All that this sutra speaks of is the unconditioned dharma. And it plainly says: all sages and worthies differ by virtue of the unconditioned dharma. Yet now, in instructing on proclaiming and on receiving and upholding, it causes one to contemplate conditioned dharmas. This is the greatest pivot of the whole sutra’s purport, and also the crucial pivot for students of the Buddha’s teaching. One should know that “unconditioned” means making no fabrication. If one makes no fabrication, how can delusion be removed? How can the true be realized? How can the ordinary be transformed? How can sagehood be attained? Therefore the unconditioned dharma must be accomplished out of the conditioned dharma. Hence it says “should contemplate.” The word “contemplate” has force. But the first essential meaning to be understood is this: the unconditioned dharma is the goal, and the conditioned dharma is the path borrowed to reach it.

To recognize only the unconditioned and to despise the conditioned is to cut oneself off; to cling to the conditioned without knowing the unconditioned is to draw a line around oneself. The former is what is called clinging to the nature and abandoning cultivation; the latter is what is called clinging to phenomena and ignoring principle. This is the second essential meaning to be understood.

To cultivate conditioned dharmas without clinging is precisely the unconditioned; apart from this there is no separately existing unconditioned dharma. Hence what this sutra says in its opening chapter—that in reality no being is liberated—must be carried out by liberating all beings; and that one should not abide in dharmas must be carried out by practicing giving. All that is said afterward has the same purport. Now, to liberate beings and practice giving are conditioned dharmas; no liberation and non-abiding in dharmas are unconditioned dharmas. Practiced thus, one is involved in existence yet does not abide in existence; one contemplates emptiness yet does not abide in emptiness. Though all day one practices the six pāramitās and the ten thousand practices, and all day expounds the sutra and speaks the Dharma, in truth one is all day in nirvana.

From this one may know: not grasping dharmas must be accomplished out of not grasping non-dharmas; “is not” must be accomplished out of “is named”; non-attachment must be accomplished out of non-annihilation; non-substantiality must be accomplished out of non-voidness; and even no-sage-and-no-ordinary is seen within sage and ordinary; the not-one and not-different is seen within one and different; the not-coming and not-going is seen within coming and going. This is what is called the one suchness of all dharmas and the equality of all dharmas. Even non-arising and non-ceasing is seen within arising and ceasing. This meaning is: though there is arising and ceasing, in truth there is no arising and ceasing; though there is no arising and ceasing, arising and ceasing is manifested. This is what is called not abiding in birth-and-death and not abiding in nirvana. Thereupon the purport of non-abiding is ultimately perfected.

And its pivot lies precisely in contemplating the conditioning of dharmas, as like a dream, like an illusion, understanding that all are empty, and thereby being non-abiding. Therefore the most essential preparatory means for a student is to contemplate thus.

To contemplate thus is to neither abolish the conditioned nor obstruct the unconditioned. Naturally and of itself, concealing and illuminating are simultaneous, and one accords with and enters, in the midst of the middle, the perfect-enlightenment sea of nature that is unmoved suchness.

A whole most profound scripture is gathered back into what is utterly plain, utterly near at hand: into a four-line verse. All sentient beings, whether of sharp or dull faculties, can accord with it and enter. This is what is called the supreme, profound, and wonderful Dharma, hard to encounter in a hundred thousand million kalpas. This is what is called true meaning.

This has the same flavor as the introductory section’s account of putting on clothes and eating food. Both point out that the Way is not far from man: it lies precisely in the ordinary affairs of daily use. One must see through them and hold firm within the ordinary affairs of daily use. Becoming a Buddha or a bodhisattva lies right therein. All the vows and practices of self-liberation and liberating others, and even such matters as bowing to the Buddha and reciting sutras, should be regarded as ordinary daily affairs, from which one does not depart even in haste or adversity, and yet one does them as though doing nothing. Only then is one near the Way.

Therefore, having gained this four-line verse, one holds not only the whole sutra but all Buddhadharma in hand; and becoming a Buddha or a bodhisattva is in hand as well. It is said that all Buddhas and the Buddhas’ anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi all come forth from this sutra. Now one knows that the Buddhas and the Dharma all come forth from contemplating all conditioned dharmas as thus and thus—like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew, or lightning.

We are fortunate to have received the Buddha’s grace and been given this wonderful method. There is nothing to do but single-mindedly follow this method, receive and uphold it thus, and proclaim it thus, so that all sentient beings may contemplate thus and all realize non-arising. Only thus can we in some small measure repay the kindness of our original teacher.

The essential purport has now been concluded. As for the similes of dream and illusion and the rest, their meaning is most refined, most subtle, most wonderful; and by practicing this contemplation one may realize the Way. Now they should be explained in detail.

There are very many similes for conditioned dharmas in the Buddhist sutras. Besides the similes of dream and illusion and the rest, there are the city of the gandharvas, the moon in water, the stake in the tree, the snake of rope, flowers in space, the horns of a hare, the hair of a tortoise, and so on. Their main purport is simply to reveal the principle that all dharmas are empty and to warn ordinary beings not to take them as real, so as to break their discrimination and attachment and lead them out of delusion. The Wei translation of the Diamond Sutra has nine similes. It says: “All conditioned dharmas are like a star, a cataract, a lamp, an illusion, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, a cloud; thus should one contemplate them.” The Qin translation reduces them to six. The number differs, but the principle is one.

Among the six similes, the dream is the general one; illusion, bubble, shadow, dew, and lightning are the particular ones. All of them serve to make clear that things are like a dream. One of good faculties, hearing the dream simile alone, can understand that dharmas produced from conditions are empty in their very substance. Fearing that some may not yet understand, the other five similes—illusion and the rest—are spoken. If the five are understood, one may suddenly realize that ten thousand things all return to one dream. What is called a dream is one of the dharmas produced from conditions. An old saying goes: what one thinks of by day takes form in dreams by night. What one thinks of is precisely the condition that produces the dream. There are also dreams that occur without any thinking of anything, such as what the world calls a message from the spirits. Then that message is also the condition for entering the dream. Hence it is a dharma produced from conditions.

Where there is a condition there must be a cause. What is the cause of dreaming? It is the consciousness—also called the false mind. Without this cause, the condition could not be met either. Hence it is said, “The perfected man has no dreams.” For a person of the Way, though the false mind is not yet cut off, he must already be able to suppress it, and so he dreams little. From this one may know that all is made by mind alone.

Pitiable are ordinary beings: in dreams they are of course the false mind, and even in what they call their waking state they are wholly the false mind as well. Therefore what they call waking is still a dream. Why? Because from beginningless time they have been deluded and have never awakened. Had they already awakened, they would certainly not merely know that the sorrow and joy, parting and meeting, gain and loss, poverty and success in dreams are false, while still taking the sorrow and joy, parting and meeting, gain and loss, poverty and success of so-called waking hours to be real. One should know that the mind in waking hours and the mind in dreams are both false and not real. Therefore the various circumstances of waking life—whether brought about by planning or arising beyond expectation—are wholly the same in principle as entering a dream either from thinking of something by day or from a spirit’s message; and their being empty in the twinkling of an eye, with nothing whatsoever obtained, is likewise in no way different. Is waking then not dreaming? Hence the warning: like a dream. Yet people cling to it in delusion, calculating and discriminating, attached and unwilling to let go. Truly this is a fool’s talk of dreams. Hence it is said that sentient beings have never awakened. To say “like a dream” now is precisely to call them to awaken quickly. Someone may say: the principle of “like a dream,” as applied to worldly dharmas, is indeed not wrong; but Chan Master Yongming Shou said, “Greatly perform the Buddha-work within a dream.” How can Buddhadharma also be contemplated as a dream? Here there are four essential meanings that must be known. Spoken with reference to ordinary beings, there are two:

(1) To contemplate Buddhadharma as a dream means not to attach. Buddhadharma lays its weight on breaking the self. If there is attachment, how can the self be broken? Therefore it should be thoroughly dispelled. Even Buddhadharma must not be attached to, how much less worldly dharmas.

(2) One who studies the Buddha’s teaching does so in order to realize the nature. If one does not realize the nature, one cannot transcend the ordinary and enter sagehood. The substance of the nature is empty and still, and so all the work of cultivation must return to nothing-attained before it accords with the empty and still nature. To contemplate Buddhadharma as a dream causes one to diligently practice the Buddha-work while returning to utter unattainability, so that subject and object may both be gone and wisdom and principle merge in the dark.
Spoken with reference to Buddhas and bodhisattvas, there are also two meanings:

(1) Buddhas and bodhisattvas are all people who have already awakened. That they greatly perform the Buddha-work, broadly liberating beings, and yet can do things as though doing nothing is because they see it all as a dream. Seeing nirvana as a dream of yesterday, they do not abide in nirvana but greatly perform the Buddha-work; seeing birth-and-death as a dream of yesterday, they do not abide in birth-and-death but constantly dwell in concentration.

(2) When a bodhisattva performs the Buddha-work, it is to awaken himself and awaken others. As for the Buddha-stage, where enlightenment is already ultimate, and yet the Buddha-work is still performed: because beings without end are still within the dream, and by the compassion of shared substance he does not consider himself ultimate, he therefore constantly practices the bodhisattva path, manifesting his body among beings who have not yet awakened from the great dream, and there performs the Buddha-work. Hence Yongming said, “Greatly perform the Buddha-work within a dream.”

Summing up these four meanings, one may know that the greatly enlightened see birth-and-death and nirvana as fundamentally unattainable. Hence it is said: birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream of yesterday. The sense is that to abide in birth-and-death is of course to dream, and to abide in nirvana is also to dream. Only when one abides nowhere at all is one greatly enlightened. Therefore, if one abides in the dharma one cultivates, in the dharma one speaks, or in the dharma one has attained, all of it is dreaming. Hence the main purport of this sutra lies in non-abiding. Therefore it says: one should practice giving without abiding anywhere; one should arouse the bodhi mind free of marks.

In sum: to contemplate all defiled and pure dharmas as a dream is intended to penetrate the truth that all conditioned dharmas are fundamentally unattainable. When the single mind is pure, what is there to attain? If there were anything attainable, it would not be pure. Therefore one should contemplate all conditioned dharmas as a dream.

Our World-Honored One taught the Dharma for forty-nine years, and yet said that no Dharma was spoken. He also said: as to anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, I attained not even the least dharma. So it is with the enlightenment of the fruition stage; and those who cultivate on the causal ground must likewise be able to know that it is so. The Śūraṅgama Sutra says: “One should carefully examine whether the mind aroused on the causal ground and the enlightenment of the fruition stage are the same or different. If on the causal ground one takes the mind of arising and ceasing as the cause of cultivation, and yet seeks the neither-arising-nor-ceasing of the Buddha-vehicle, there is no such possibility.” To have something attainable is the mind of arising and ceasing; to contemplate it as a dream, utterly unattainable, is neither arising nor ceasing. One should know that a dream is precisely a conditioned dharma. If one knows that the dream is utterly unattainable and does not deludedly cling, the conditioned dharma becomes the unconditioned dharma.

The word “like” has flavor. For the unawakened, one should contemplate that what they call waking is still like a dream, and only then can one be liberated from all and keep far from inversion. For the awakened, one should contemplate that what they call enlightenment is likewise like a dream; what harm then in entering the land of Huaxu and sporting in samādhi?

In sum, the six similes are all carried through to the very end. They are not spoken for ordinary beings alone. If the followers of the Two Vehicles know that liberating beings is like a dream, utterly unattainable, they will not sink into emptiness and stagnate in quiescence. If a certain class of bodhisattvas knows that seeking above and transforming below is like a dream, utterly unattainable, they can accomplish Buddhahood. Therefore to practice the contemplation of dream is precisely the precious mirror that illumines and breaks the two attachments, to self and to dharmas, and the compassionate ship that carries one across into the great sea of quiescent extinction.

From what has been said above, one may know that all conditioned dharmas are fruits produced when mind is taken as the cause, affairs are relied on as the conditions, and cause and condition meet. Apart from cause and effect there is nothing at all. Yet what is named a fruit in turn becomes a cause; what is called a cause presently summons a fruit again. Even of cause and effect themselves, then, there is no fixed form whatever. Hence it is said that they are empty in their very substance. Take dreaming: it is not that the affairs and marks are not plainly there, yet their existence is no existence. Hence it is said that dharmas produced from cause and condition are precisely provisional and precisely empty. Therefore one simile of the dream is enough to penetrate all.

But because sentient beings have long been on the deluded path, though in ordinary times they cannot but know that worldly affairs are like a dream, yet the moment a favorable or unfavorable circumstance appears before them they still cling in delusion and cannot let go. They even say: past affairs are indeed like a dream, but when circumstances are present and one experiences them distinctly in one’s own person, can one call them unreal? Therefore the Buddha further tells them: though favorable and unfavorable circumstances are distinctly experienced in one’s own person, in truth they are all like an illusion. An illusion is the magic art spoken of in the Buddhist sutras; in the present age it is called a play. The sense is: have you seen a magician and his magic? He conjures forth all kinds of flying, swimming, moving, and growing things—are they not plainly like the real? Or again, like a stage play: when the actors put on their paint and mount the stage, the wicked and the upright, the worthy and the foolish, sorrow and joy, gain and loss, their expressions come vividly to life, and can make one’s face brighten and one’s tears fall. Do you take that as real too? Would you, because their sorrow and joy are without cause and seem to be experienced in your own person, insist that it is actual fact? One should know that living in the world is the same: all that one encounters is nothing but the transformation of false consciousness and karmic conditions.

The world is a theater! All sentient beings are the various roles in the theater. When the gongs and drums are loud and the clamor is at its height, one who has wisdom should warn himself: in the twinkling of an eye one steps down from the stage. To play this role here and now is only to be pulled along by the power of karma and to finish out a stretch of karmic affinity—how could one take it as real? Just as in an opera, once one has become an actor in the play, there must be a former cause for this present fruit to appear. Of course one cannot but sing and act with all one’s heart, lest the aim one holds be missed. Yet there is certainly no one who clings to the character played in the opera and takes it as himself. What is the actor’s aim? Fame and money. So too with being a person. To come in this life and be this person is only to fill for a while one role in this play. The actor can still avoid clinging to the character he plays and taking him as himself; how can we mistake the role we temporarily fill for ourselves? One should know that cause and effect are hard to escape and are to be feared. Since one temporarily fills this role, one naturally cannot but sing and act with all one’s heart, lest the aim be missed. But one must never take fame and profit alone as the aim; one must recognize clearly one’s own inherent family treasure as the aim. What is the family treasure? It is the three jewels of the self-nature.

One must clearly awaken to this: in playing out this false play, one must neither mistake cause and effect and drag down the self-nature, nor mistake the false play for the real and lose the self-nature. Therefore, just when the music is loud and clear and the whole audience is watching, one should awaken oneself and realize: this act of illusory play is not my original face. One should vow to return to one’s first garments. Only then, when the gongs and drums fall silent and the wind blows the clouds apart, will one not be vexed and grieved, at a loss what to do with one’s hands and feet. Hence it is said that one should contemplate as an illusion.

The World-Honored One in his great compassion still feared that beings, clinging in delusion, would not awaken, thinking that though all human affairs may indeed be like an illusion, yet when one considers one’s own body and life it is in the end hard to let go. For in their minds they can understand that worldly affairs are like an illusion, yet they still take the vast world and their precious physical body to be truly existent, and so cannot let go. Therefore the Buddha further tells them: like a bubble, like a shadow. “Like a bubble” is a simile for the world; “like a shadow” is a simile for the physical body. Why? What is called a bubble is formed when water is stirred by wind and dashed into foam; and the world is formed by all sentient beings, within the sea of nature, raising the wind of ignorance and creating this shared karma, which then congeals. Hence it is likened to a bubble.
