What is called a shadow appears when the sun, moon, or lamplight shines upon something; and the physical body is transformed and manifested from the light of the nature. Hence it is likened to a shadow. Since this world and this body are of the same conditioned production as bubble and shadow, one can see that body and world are likewise of the same falseness as bubble and shadow. How can one deludedly take them as real?

This meaning is stated most clearly in the Śūraṅgama Sutra. It says: “Acknowledging delusion within enlightenment, one makes of it a murky void. Within the murky void, one knits darkness into form. Form mixed with false thought, the thought-mark becomes the body.” This passage says that the enlightened nature, perfect and bright, is great beyond any outside and small beyond any inside. Originally there is no such thing as empty space, a world, or a physical body; all come about because sentient beings’ enlightened nature is obstructed, so that what was originally perfect and bright becomes murky. What is murky is the dizzy, turbid appearance. Since one has already failed to awaken, one instead takes the murky as empty space. Hence “one makes of it a murky void.” This comes from acknowledging delusion within enlightenment. “Acknowledging delusion within enlightenment” means that one supposes oneself enlightened when in fact one is still deluded. Why? Because one takes the murky for empty space. Since empty space is murky, one further knots this darkness into form. Hence, “within the murky void, one knits darkness into form.” Form means the four great elements, earth, water, fire, and wind. It refers precisely to the world and to all the marks of material form, sentient and insentient. First one takes the murky as empty space, then one takes the darkness knotted together as the world, and further one takes what is mixed of form and false thought as one’s precious body. Hence, “form mixed with false thought, the thought-mark becomes the body.” The word “acknowledging” in the first line runs straight through to the end. The two words “false thought” also run through the whole passage, above and below.

Why does one mistakenly acknowledge? Because there is false thought. False thought is another name for consciousness. Feeling, perception, and mental formation are mental factors of consciousness; therefore the words “false thought” here refer to the four aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formation, and consciousness among the five aggregates. The “mark” in “the thought-mark becomes the body” is the word “form” above; “thought” is false thought. The bodies of all sentient beings are nothing but a provisional union of the five aggregates. Hence it says: “form mixed with false thought, the thought-mark becomes the body”—meaning that the marks of form of the four great elements are mixed and joined with the false thoughts of feeling, perception, mental formation, and consciousness to form this illusory body. This passage plainly teaches that empty space, the world, and the physical body are all transformed and manifested from sentient beings’ dizzy, turbid false thoughts. False thoughts are themselves unreal and cease and arise in an instant. How could the body and world they manifest be real?

Everyone knows that a bubble in water is extremely frail and thinnest, most easily destroyed. They do not realize that the world is the same. Let no one say that rivers and mountains endure through the ages. Though the whole world may not be destroyed all at once, yet hills sink into valleys and valleys rise into hills, mulberry fields become the sea and the sea becomes mulberry fields, and changes arise from time to time. This is enough to prove that it is at every moment within formation and destruction. This is a matter that those of somewhat greater years have constantly experienced; it is no mere speculative talk.

Moreover the Śūraṅgama Sutra says: “Space is born within the great enlightenment, like a single bubble rising in the sea. The outflows’ countries of fine dust all depend on space and are born. When the bubble bursts, space is originally nothing—how much less the three existences.” “Outflows” makes clear that they must perish; “fine dust” makes clear that they are exceedingly minute. “The three existences” means the three realms. This passage says that the murky void is within the great sea of perfect enlightenment like a single bubble on the sea—bubble meaning foam. And the countries of fine dust are still more things clinging to the bubble of the sea. When the bubble bursts, there is not even the murky void, much less the three realms. All students should constantly contemplate this principle. The void that one acknowledges is still a murky, dizzy, turbid appearance, and is itself as tiny as a bubble. How much less the world, how much less this body—what are they worth counting? How can one cast aside the true, perfect, and bright sea of nature, which contains the void and encompasses the three realms, and acknowledge instead a tiny, frail, impermanent floating bubble?

As for a shadow: looked at from afar it seems to exist; examined in fact, it is nothing. This body is the same: it falsely appears to exist, but examined in fact it is nothing. For example, a person’s reflection in a mirror appears when it is reflected; fat or thin, long or short, not the least bit is off. This body is the same: because the mind creates karma, it appears following karma; long life or early death, beauty or ugliness, cause and effect are hard to escape. Great Master Si of Nanyue said: the pure mind is like a mirror, ordinary and sage are like the images. This makes clear that the body is visible because the pure mind inherently possesses the nature of seeing, just as an image is visible because a bright mirror inherently possesses the nature of reflecting. How can one, because it is visible, mistakenly take it as truly existent? Moreover, within the seeing-nature of the pure mind there is originally no such body; it is merely a shadow manifested by the seeing-nature. It is also like the reflecting nature of a bright mirror, within which there is originally no such image; it is merely a shadow manifested by the reflecting nature. All that has been said above still takes the illusory body as viewed from the pure mind, making clear that it is a shadow manifested by the pure mind. If one speaks in terms of the illusory body in its very substance, it is likewise like a shadow. Why? Because apart from the five aggregates it is utterly unattainable. And moreover the form among the five aggregates is precisely the four great elements; since the four great elements are like a floating bubble, the remaining four aggregates—feeling, perception, mental formation, and consciousness—are likewise nothing but false. (They are called false thoughts, hence false.) Thus the five aggregates themselves are already utterly unattainable; how much less the illusory body, provisionally joined of the five aggregates—its seeming existence and actual nonexistence can be known. “Utterly unattainable” means that its existence is no existence. It is exactly like a shadow, which merely dazzles and deceives the eye; in truth it is originally empty.

What all ordinary beings most cling to as truly existent are the consciousness-mind, the world, and their own bodies. Now each is refuted in turn: the consciousness-mind is like an illusion (it was said earlier that the world is a theater and all beings are the roles in the theater, all nothing but the transformation of consciousness-mind and karmic conditions—hence “like an illusion”), the world is like a bubble, and this body is like a shadow. If body, mind, and world are still false and unreal, then all other conditioned marks of dharmas may be known likewise. Yet beings on the deluded path, though they know that body, mind, and world are unreal, may still drift along in negligence and fail to diligently practice the contemplation of dream, illusion, bubble, and shadow. Therefore they are again roused and spurred: like dew, like lightning. Dew dries at sunrise and does not remain long; lightning arises and ceases in a flash, passing in an instant. It is as is said, life lies within a breath. One should press on with one’s practice as though putting out a fire on one’s head. Taken together with the five similes of illusion and the rest, this is to contemplate that all things are like a dream, existing yet not existing. Hence it is said: the five contemplations of illusion and the rest are particular; the contemplation of dream is general.
